chunk_findings.detail: When `[submodules].verify_tree = "refuse"`, a worktree whose submodule state cannot be listed is returned as a plain warning string instead of an `O.refused` outcome. For example, if the bound worktree’s `.git` pointer is broken or `git submodule status` fails, `SS.detect(tree)` returns `None`; `tree_check` then returns `f"submodule check not run in {tree}: ..."`. The caller treats a `str` as a warning (as `claim_warnings` does) and does not undo the claim, so a claim against a worktree with uninitialized/broken submodules remains active despite the configured `refuse` mode.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/claim_submodules.py:tree_check (line 34)

chunk_findings.detail: In `[submodules].cross_lease = "refuse"` mode, a detection failure is downgraded to a non-fatal `Note`. If `SS.detect(ctx.repo)` returns `None` because git cannot list submodules (e.g., corrupt git metadata, missing git binary, unreadable `.git`), `_check_submodules` returns a `Note` rather than `O.refused`. Thus a lease whose globs actually cross a submodule is allowed through with only a warning, even though the knob description says `refuse` turns the claim away.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/claim_guard_submodules.py:_check_submodules (line 30)

chunk_findings.detail: When `SS.detect(tree)` returns `None` (git cannot list submodules), the function calls `O.nothing("submodules", f"git could not list...", text="", submodules=[])`. In this module the other outcome constructors use `text` for the human-readable outcome text (`O.ok(..., text=...)` and `O.failed(..., text)`), so the second positional argument to `O.nothing` binds the same `text` parameter that is then supplied again as the keyword `text=""`. Given a repository where `git submodule status` fails (e.g. corrupt gitdir), the intended exit-2 “could not tell” path raises `TypeError` instead of returning that outcome.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/submodules.py:28

chunk_findings.detail: The submodule path is treated as a literal prefix in `_is_inside` but is passed unescaped as a glob pattern to `GL.overlap` in `_spans`. Given a submodule whose path literally contains a glob metacharacter, e.g. `vendor/?`, the lease glob `vendor/?/**` is classified as inside because `_is_inside` sees the literal prefix `vendor/?/` and returns no crossing. But as a glob, `?` matches any single character, so the same glob also matches paths outside the submodule such as `vendor/x/file`; that is a crossing and should be refused. The same lack of escaping can also produce false crossings: for submodule `vendor/?`, `GL.overlap("vendor/x/file", "vendor/?/**")` treats the literal `?` in the submodule path as a wildcard and reports a crossing for a glob that is outside the submodule. This can silently mis-scope a lease across a submodule boundary.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/submodules.py:_is_inside/_spans

chunk_findings.detail: `cross_refusal` assumes there is only one crossed submodule. It sorts the crossed submodules and uses only `subs[0]` in the suggested fix: `ddflow update {item}-inner --globs {first}/**` and `ddflow update {item}-outer --globs <the rest>`. If a claim crosses two or more submodules, e.g. item globs `**` with submodules `a` and `b`, the generated commands still leave `b` in the outer item’s lease, so the outer lease would still cross a submodule boundary. That contradicts the docstring’s promise that the words name “the calls that get past it”.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/submodule_text.py:42

chunk_findings.detail: The shell commands generated by `cross_refusal` interpolate `item` and `first` without quoting or escaping. Git submodule paths may contain spaces. For a submodule path `my sub`, the refusal tells the user to run `ddflow update item-inner --globs my sub/**`, which a shell parses as two globs, `my` and `sub/**`, not the intended single glob. The suggested next call is therefore wrong for valid submodule paths containing spaces.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/submodule_text.py:42

chunk_findings.detail: `fix` builds shell command strings by interpolating `tree` and `self.path` directly, but the docstring calls the result “the exact next call.” Given a worktree at `/tmp/my repo` and an uninitialized submodule `sub`, the uninitialised branch returns `git -C /tmp/my repo submodule update --init --recursive`; run in a shell, `git -C` sees `/tmp/my` as the worktree and `repo` as another argument, so the command fails. The pointer branch has the same problem for `rm {Path(tree) / self.path / '.git'}`, and unquoted paths can also execute shell metacharacters if a caller treats the returned string as a command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/submodules.py:Problem.fix

chunk_findings.detail: The tree-check description contradicts the knob description. Line 34 says a failing tree check causes the claim to be undone, but line 37 says `verify_tree=warn` claims and only prints a warning. Concrete input: operator sets `ddflow config submodules.verify_tree warn --local`, then claims an item whose submodule is not initialised. The document simultaneously specifies that the claim is undone and that the claim proceeds with a warning, leaving the intended behavior ambiguous.
chunk_findings.title: docs/guide/submodules.md:34

chunk_findings.detail: The test treats a lease whose only glob is `["vendor/lib"]` as “wholly inside” the submodule and asserts `CS.crossings(["vendor/lib"], [SUB]) == []`. But `vendor/lib` is the submodule path itself, which in Git is a parent-repository gitlink entry, not a file or directory wholly inside the submodule. A task/claim scoped to `vendor/lib` can therefore pass the cross-boundary guard and then stage/commit a submodule-pointer change in the parent repo without a paired submodule item, which is exactly the cross-boundary case the change says must be refused. The expectation should be a crossing/boundary refusal for the exact submodule path, not an empty crossing list.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_submodule_detect.py:34

chunk_findings.detail: `declared()` treats any non-regular-file `.gitmodules` as “no submodules.” If the repository root contains a directory named `.gitmodules` (or a broken symlink, or a path whose stat fails), `Path(repo) / ".gitmodules").is_file()` is false and the function returns `{}` without asking git. The module contract says `None` means “git could not tell,” so callers are allowed to interpret `{}` as “there are no declared submodules.” For example, a checkout with a stray `.gitmodules/` directory and a submodule gitlink under `vendor/foo` (or with `gitlinks()` unavailable/timed out) will be seen as having zero declared submodules; a lease glob such as `vendor/**` can then be treated as clear of a submodule boundary, producing the silent mis-scoping this change is meant to prevent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/git_submodules.py:27

chunk_findings.detail: With the default `verify_tree = "refuse"`, this function is supposed to undo the claim when the bound worktree has a submodule problem. But when `SS.detect(tree)` returns `None`—for example because the worktree’s `.git` pointer is broken, missing, or otherwise unusable, which is exactly one of the conditions the change says must “fail loudly”—the code returns the warning string `"submodule check not run in ...: git could not list its submodules"`. The caller’s type contract treats a `str` as a warning and only treats an `O.Outcome` as a refusal, so the claim remains active with merely a warning. A claim on a worktree containing an empty submodule directory can therefore proceed and later mis-scope submodule operations into the parent repository despite `verify_tree = "refuse"`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/claim_submodules.py:tree_check

chunk_findings.detail: When `cross_lease = "refuse"` (the default), a lease whose globs cross a submodule should be refused. If `SS.detect(ctx.repo)` returns `None`—for example because `.gitmodules` is malformed, unreadable, or a git invocation fails—the guard does not run `CS.crossings` and does not return `O.refused`; it only returns a `Note`. Given a repository that actually contains a submodule such as `vendor/lib`, a claim with globs like `vendor/**` will be allowed through with a warning, so the default “refuse” safety gate is bypassed whenever the submodule list cannot be read.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/claim_guard_submodules.py:_check_submodules

chunk_findings.detail: When `SS.detect(tree)` returns `None` (git could not list the submodules), `submodules_view` returns an outcome whose payload still contains `submodules=[]`. In the ordinary “no submodules” case, `SS.detect` returns `[]` and the function also returns `submodules=[]` in `O.ok`. Given a repo or recorded tree where git is unavailable or the tree is not a valid git worktree, an MCP/automation client that reads the `submodules` field sees the same empty list as it would for a repository with no submodules and may proceed as if there is no submodule boundary. That contradicts the stated safety rule that “could not tell” must never be represented as “no submodules”; the unknown case should fail or otherwise omit/flag the submodule list instead of returning an empty one.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/submodules.py:27

chunk_findings.detail: `inside()` accepts `globs: Iterable[str]` but does not materialize it before the nested scan. If the caller passes a generator or any one-shot iterator, the first submodule consumes it and later submodule paths see an empty glob list. For example, `inside(iter(["vendor/lib/**", "vendor/other/**"]), ["vendor/lib", "vendor/other"])` returns only `{"vendor/lib": ["vendor/lib/**"]}` and omits `vendor/other`, even though the second glob is wholly inside the second submodule. This is inconsistent with `crossings()`, which explicitly does `list(globs)`, and can silently under-report submodule membership for multi-submodule repositories.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/submodules.py:inside

chunk_findings.detail: When `cross` contains crossings for more than one submodule, the generated remediation only handles `subs[0]`. For example, if a lease crosses submodules `vendor/a` and `vendor/b`, the refusal tells the operator to split into `item-outer`/`item-inner`, set the inner globs to `vendor/a/**`, and put `<the rest>` in the outer item. If `<the rest>` includes `vendor/b/**`, the outer lease still crosses `vendor/b`, so the suggested calls do not get past the refusal. The function has the full set of crossed submodules but emits exact next calls for only one of them.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/submodule_text.py:31 `cross_refusal`

chunk_findings.detail: The command strings interpolate the submodule path without shell quoting. Given a submodule path containing spaces, such as `vendor/my lib`, the emitted command is `ddflow update item-inner --globs vendor/my lib/**`, which a shell parses as two globs (`vendor/my` and `lib/**`), causing the operator to claim the wrong files. If the path contains shell metacharacters, copying the suggested command can also execute unintended shell commands.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/submodule_text.py:41 `cross_refusal`

chunk_findings.detail: `fix` interpolates `tree` and `self.path` directly into a shell command. With `tree=Path("/tmp/my repo")` and a submodule path `"vendor"`, a `pointer` problem returns `rm /tmp/my repo/vendor/.git && git -C /tmp/my repo submodule update --init --recursive`; a shell parses that as `rm` with operands `/tmp/my` and `repo/vendor/.git` (relative to the current directory) and `git -C /tmp/my repo ...`. This can delete the wrong paths and run the update in the wrong repository. Paths containing spaces, `$`, backticks, `;`, etc. make the returned “exact next call” incorrect or injectable; the operands must be quoted or the command should be built as an argv list.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/submodules.py:Problem.fix (lines 42-48)

chunk_findings.detail: For an uninitialised submodule whose directory already contains files, `_state` returns a `uninitialised` problem, but `fix` still returns `git -C {tree} submodule update --init --recursive`. If `.gitmodules` declares `vendor`, the index has a gitlink for `vendor`, and `tree/vendor` contains `README` but no `.git`, that command attempts to clone/update into an existing non-empty submodule directory and git refuses (`fatal: ... already exists and is not an empty directory`). Thus the returned command is not the exact command that fixes the reported problem for the non-empty case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/submodules.py:Problem.fix (lines 42, 50)

chunk_findings.detail: The command is documented and grouped as an action of the `ddflow_view` MCP tool (`family="ddflow_view"`, `action="submodules"`), but it sets `tool="ddflow_submodules"`. chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/submodules.py:27

chunk_findings.detail: The guide states the two knobs are operator-only and that weakening them is refused “for the committed config”, with only the local layer allowed. That makes a project or org committed config such as `[submodules] cross_lease = "warn"` unusable. The change’s stated D-universal-principles conformance requires every knob/default to be settable by file, CLI, MCP, and prompt and overridable per project and per org [r-everything-configurable]; refusing committed config is a defect.

chunk_findings.detail: The module bootstraps imports by inserting only the repository root (`parents[1]`) into `sys.path`, then imports sibling test helpers as top-level modules (`conftest`, `submodule_fixture`). If the `tests` directory is not already on `sys.path` — for example under `pytest --import-mode=importlib`, or if `tests/` is a package so pytest inserts the repository root rather than the test directory — collection fails at the `from conftest import ...` / `from submodule_fixture import ...` lines with `ModuleNotFoundError` for `conftest` or `submodule_fixture`. chunk_findings.detail: The new `_literal(sub)` is only applied to the overlap pattern; `_is_inside(glob, sub)` still compares against the raw submodule path, so submodule paths containing glob metacharacters are not read literally for the “is this glob inside the submodule?” test. Conversely, the unescaped glob `vendor/*/**` is treated as inside because it starts with the raw `vendor/*/`, even though its `*` also matches other immediate children such as `vendor/other/file`, so a crossing lease is not refused.

chunk_findings.detail: `_pair_calls` constructs the suggested inner-item glob as `sub + "/**"` and then only applies `shlex.quote`. chunk_findings.detail: The new `stray` remediation chooses `"<submodule path>.stray"` as the move-aside target without checking for collision. If the repository has both a stray submodule `vendor` and a real submodule `vendor.stray`, the generated command is `mv vendor vendor.stray && ...`. POSIX `mv` treats an existing directory target as a directory to move *into*, so this succeeds and leaves the stray files under `vendor.stray/vendor`, i.e. inside another submodule’s worktree, before running `git submodule update --init --recursive`. That can silently pollute or mis-scope `vendor.stray`; if `vendor.stray` is a file, the command instead fails.

In the same glob dialect used by the preceding line, `[b]` is a character class matching only `b`, and `?` matches exactly one character, so the pattern matches paths under `vendor/liXb/`, not paths under the literal submodule directory `vendor/li?[b]/`. Given a repository with that submodule and a lease intended to touch the sibling `vendor/liXb`, this assertion locks in a refusal of a glob that cannot reach the submodule at all, contradicting the stated rule that only leases whose globs cross a submodule path should be refused.

chunk_findings.detail: When `_aside` cannot find a free sibling, `Problem.fix` returns `mv -- '<stray>' <a free name> && git -C ...`. chunk_findings.detail: The submodule path is treated as a literal prefix in `_is_inside` but is passed unescaped as a glob pattern to `GL.overlap` in `_spans`. Given a submodule whose path literally contains a glob metacharacter, e.g. `vendor/?`, the lease glob `vendor/?/**` is classified as inside because `_is_inside` sees the literal prefix `vendor/?/` and returns no crossing. chunk_findings.detail: The test treats a lease whose only glob is `["vendor/lib"]` as “wholly inside” the submodule and asserts `CS.crossings(["vendor/lib"], [SUB]) == []`. But `vendor/lib` is the submodule path itself, which in Git is a parent-repository gitlink entry, not a file or directory wholly inside the submodule. A task/claim scoped to `vendor/lib` can therefore pass the cross-boundary guard and then stage/commit a submodule-pointer change in the parent repo without a paired submodule item, which is exactly the cross-boundary case the change says must be refused. The expectation should be a crossing/boundary refusal for the exact submodule path, not an empty crossing list.

chunk_findings.detail: The previous “wildcard submodule path” fix is still incomplete: `_spans` now escapes the submodule path only for `GL.overlap`, but `_is_inside` still treats the raw glob string as a literal prefix. Given a submodule whose path literally contains `?`, e.g. `vendor/?`, and a lease glob `["vendor/?/**"]`, `_is_inside("vendor/?/**", "vendor/?")` returns true because the string starts with `vendor/?/`, so `_spans` short-circuits and no crossing is reported. The glob engine, however, reads `?` as a single-character wildcard, so the same lease also matches parent-repo paths such as `vendor/x/file`; a claim can stage/commit those outside-submodule files without a paired submodule item, silently crossing the boundary. The new `_literal` escaping in `_spans` does not answer this because the inside check prevents `_spans` from being reached.

chunk_findings.detail: The paired-items commands quote the submodule glob only for the shell, not for ddflow’s glob engine. Given a valid submodule path containing a glob metacharacter, e.g. `vendor/?`, `_pair_calls` emits `ddflow update item-inner --globs 'vendor/?/**'`. The single quotes prevent shell expansion, but ddflow still receives the pattern `vendor/?/**`, where `?` is a one-character wildcard, so the suggested inner item can match files outside the submodule such as `vendor/x/file`. Thus the refusal’s “exact next calls” can still create a cross-boundary item; the path should be escaped/literalized for glob matching before appending `/**`, as the core `_literal` change in this same change does.

chunk_findings.detail: `shlex.quote` prevents word splitting and globbing, but it does not stop the next command from treating a path argument that begins with `-` as an option. For a valid relative worktree path such as `tree = Path('-repo')` and a submodule path `sub`, the new `stray` branch returns `mv '-repo/sub' '-repo/sub.stray' && git -C '-repo' submodule update --init --recursive`. After shell quoting is removed, `mv` receives `-repo/sub` as an argv beginning with `-` and parses it as an option rather than a pathname, so the command fails instead of being “the exact next call.” The same class of problem applies to the generated `rm` and `git submodule add`/`git rm --cached` path operands; they need `--` (or a `./`-prefixed path) in addition to quoting.

chunk_findings.detail: `_aside` is documented to return a “free sibling name”, but its fallback is not checked for existence. When the first 99 candidates are occupied, `range(1, _ASIDE_TRIES)` exits and the function returns `where.with_name(f"{where.name}.stray{_ASIDE_TRIES}")` without testing whether that path already exists. For example, if a stray submodule path is a file `vendor/lib` and the files `vendor/lib.stray`, `vendor/lib.stray2`, …, `vendor/lib.stray100` all exist, `_aside` returns `vendor/lib.stray100`; the emitted `mv -- vendor/lib vendor/lib.stray100` then overwrites the existing file. This defeats the “move stray files aside” safety goal and can silently destroy or mis-place user data.

chunk_findings.detail: `declared()` treats any non-regular-file `.gitmodules` as “no submodules.” If the repository root contains a directory named `.gitmodules` (or a broken symlink, or a path whose stat fails), `Path(repo) / ".gitmodules").is_file()` is false and the function returns `{}` without asking git. The module contract says `None` means “git could not tell,” so callers are allowed to interpret `{}` as “there are no declared submodules.” For example, a checkout with a stray `.gitmodules/` directory and a submodule gitlink under `vendor/foo` (or with `gitlinks()` unavailable/timed out) will be seen as having zero declared submodules; a lease glob such as `vendor/**` can then be treated as clear of a submodule boundary, producing the silent mis-scoping this change is meant to prevent.

chunk_findings.detail: With the default `verify_tree = "refuse"`, this function is supposed to undo the claim when the bound worktree has a submodule problem. But when `SS.detect(tree)` returns `None`—for example because the worktree’s `.git` pointer is broken, missing, or otherwise unusable, which is exactly one of the conditions the change says must “fail loudly”—the code returns the warning string `"submodule check not run in ...: git could not list its submodules"`. The caller’s type contract treats a `str` as a warning and only treats an `O.Outcome` as a refusal, so the claim remains active with merely a warning. A claim on a worktree containing an empty submodule directory can therefore proceed and later mis-scope submodule operations into the parent repository despite `verify_tree = "refuse"`.

chunk_findings.detail: When `cross_lease = "refuse"` (the default), a lease whose globs cross a submodule should be refused. If `SS.detect(ctx.repo)` returns `None`—for example because `.gitmodules` is malformed, unreadable, or a git invocation fails—the guard does not run `CS.crossings` and does not return `O.refused`; it only returns a `Note`. Given a repository that actually contains a submodule such as `vendor/lib`, a claim with globs like `vendor/**` will be allowed through with a warning, so the default “refuse” safety gate is bypassed whenever the submodule list cannot be read.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/claim_guard_submodules.py:_check_submodules

chunk_findings.detail: When `SS.detect(tree)` returns `None` (git could not list the submodules), `submodules_view` returns an outcome whose payload still contains `submodules=[]`. In the ordinary “no submodules” case, `SS.detect` returns `[]` and the function also returns `submodules=[]` in `O.ok`. Given a repo or recorded tree where git is unavailable or the tree is not a valid git worktree, an MCP/automation client that reads the `submodules` field sees the same empty list as it would for a repository with no submodules and may proceed as if there is no submodule boundary. That contradicts the stated safety rule that “could not tell” must never be represented as “no submodules”; the unknown case should fail or otherwise omit/flag the submodule list instead of returning an empty one.

chunk_findings.detail: `inside()` accepts `globs: Iterable[str]` but does not materialize it before the nested scan. If the caller passes a generator or any one-shot iterator, the first submodule consumes it and later submodule paths see an empty glob list. For example, `inside(iter(["vendor/lib/**", "vendor/other/**"]), ["vendor/lib", "vendor/other"])` returns only `{"vendor/lib": ["vendor/lib/**"]}` and omits `vendor/other`, even though the second glob is wholly inside the second submodule. This is inconsistent with `crossings()`, which explicitly does `list(globs)`, and can silently under-report submodule membership for multi-submodule repositories.

If `<the rest>` includes `vendor/b/**`, the outer lease still crosses `vendor/b`, so the suggested calls do not get past the refusal. The function has the full set of crossed submodules but emits exact next calls for only one of them.

chunk_findings.detail: `declared()` treats any non-regular-file `.gitmodules` as “no submodules.” If the repository root contains a directory named `.gitmodules` (or a broken symlink, or a path whose stat fails), `Path(repo) / ".gitmodules").is_file()` is false and the function returns `{}` without asking git. chunk_findings.detail: With the default `verify_tree = "refuse"`, this function is supposed to undo the claim when the bound worktree has a submodule problem. But when `SS.detect(tree)` returns `None`—for example because the worktree’s `.git` pointer is broken, missing, or otherwise unusable, which is exactly one of the conditions the change says must “fail loudly”—the code returns the warning string `"submodule check not run in ...: git could not list its submodules"`. The caller’s type contract treats a `str` as a warning and only treats an `O.Outcome` as a refusal, so the claim remains active with merely a warning. A claim on a worktree containing an empty submodule directory can therefore proceed and later mis-scope submodule operations into the parent repository despite `verify_tree = "refuse"`.

chunk_findings.detail: When `cross_lease = "refuse"` (the default), a lease whose globs cross a submodule should be refused. If `SS.detect(ctx.repo)` returns `None`—for example because `.gitmodules` is malformed, unreadable, or a git invocation fails—the guard does not run `CS.crossings` and does not return `O.refused`; it only returns a `Note`. Given a repository that actually contains a submodule such as `vendor/lib`, a claim with globs like `vendor/**` will be allowed through with a warning, so the default “refuse” safety gate is bypassed whenever the submodule list cannot be read.

chunk_findings.detail: When `SS.detect(tree)` returns `None` (git could not list the submodules), `submodules_view` returns an outcome whose payload still contains `submodules=[]`. In the ordinary “no submodules” case, `SS.detect` returns `[]` and the function also returns `submodules=[]` in `O.ok`. Given a repo or recorded tree where git is unavailable or the tree is not a valid git worktree, an MCP/automation client that reads the `submodules` field sees the same empty list as it would for a repository with no submodules and may proceed as if there is no submodule boundary. That contradicts the stated safety rule that “could not tell” must never be represented as “no submodules”; the unknown case should fail or otherwise omit/flag the submodule list instead of returning an empty one.

chunk_findings.detail: `inside()` accepts `globs: Iterable[str]` but does not materialize it before the nested scan. If the caller passes a generator or any one-shot iterator, the first submodule consumes it and later submodule paths see an empty glob list. This is inconsistent with `crossings()`, which explicitly does `list(globs)`, and can silently under-report submodule membership for multi-submodule repositories.

chunk_findings.detail: `declared()` treats any non-regular-file `.gitmodules` as “no submodules.” If the repository root contains a directory named `.gitmodules` (or a broken symlink, or a path whose stat fails), `Path(repo) / ".gitmodules").is_file()` is false and the function returns `{}` without asking git. The module contract says `None` means “git could not tell,” so callers are allowed to interpret `{}` as “there are no declared submodules.” For example, a checkout with a stray `.gitmodules/` directory and a submodule gitlink under `vendor/foo` (or with `gitlinks()` unavailable/timed out) will be seen as having zero declared submodules; a lease glob such as `vendor/**` can then be treated as clear of a submodule boundary, producing the silent mis-scoping this change is meant to prevent.

chunk_findings.detail: With the default `verify_tree = "refuse"`, this function is supposed to undo the claim when the bound worktree has a submodule problem. But when `SS.detect(tree)` returns `None`—for example because the worktree’s `.git` pointer is broken, missing, or otherwise unusable, which is exactly one of the conditions the change says must “fail loudly”—the code returns the warning string `"submodule check not run in ...: git could not list its submodules"`. The caller’s type contract treats a `str` as a warning and only treats an `O.Outcome` as a refusal, so the claim remains active with merely a warning. A claim on a worktree containing an empty submodule directory can therefore proceed and later mis-scope submodule operations into the parent repository despite `verify_tree = "refuse"`.

chunk_findings.detail: When `cross_lease = "refuse"` (the default), a lease whose globs cross a submodule should be refused. If `SS.detect(ctx.repo)` returns `None`—for example because `.gitmodules` is malformed, unreadable, or a git invocation fails—the guard does not run `CS.crossings` and does not return `O.refused`; it only returns a `Note`. Given a repository that actually contains a submodule such as `vendor/lib`, a claim with globs like `vendor/**` will be allowed through with a warning, so the default “refuse” safety gate is bypassed whenever the submodule list cannot be read.

chunk_findings.detail: When `SS.detect(tree)` returns `None` (git could not list the submodules), `submodules_view` returns an outcome whose payload still contains `submodules=[]`. In the ordinary “no submodules” case, `SS.detect` returns `[]` and the function also returns `submodules=[]` in `O.ok`. Given a repo or recorded tree where git is unavailable or the tree is not a valid git worktree, an MCP/automation client that reads the `submodules` field sees the same empty list as it would for a repository with no submodules and may proceed as if there is no submodule boundary. That contradicts the stated safety rule that “could not tell” must never be represented as “no submodules”; the unknown case should fail or otherwise omit/flag the submodule list instead of returning an empty one.

chunk_findings.detail: `inside()` accepts `globs: Iterable[str]` but does not materialize it before the nested scan. If the caller passes a generator or any one-shot iterator, the first submodule consumes it and later submodule paths see an empty glob list. For example, `inside(iter(["vendor/lib/**", "vendor/other/**"]), ["vendor/lib", "vendor/other"])` returns only `{"vendor/lib": ["vendor/lib/**"]}` and omits `vendor/other`, even though the second glob is wholly inside the second submodule. This is inconsistent with `crossings()`, which explicitly does `list(globs)`, and can silently under-report submodule membership for multi-submodule repositories.

chunk_findings.detail: When `cross` contains crossings for more than one submodule, the generated remediation only handles `subs[0]`. If `<the rest>` includes `vendor/b/**`, the outer lease still crosses `vendor/b`, so the suggested calls do not get past the refusal. The function has the full set of crossed submodules but emits exact next calls for only one of them.

chunk_findings.detail: `fix` interpolates `tree` and `self.path` directly into a shell command. With `tree=Path("/tmp/my repo")` and a submodule path `"vendor"`, a `pointer` problem returns `rm /tmp/my repo/vendor/.git && git -C /tmp/my repo submodule update --init --recursive`; a shell parses that as `rm` with operands `/tmp/my` and `repo/vendor/.git` (relative to the current directory) and `git -C /tmp/my repo ...`. This can delete the wrong paths and run the update in the wrong repository. Paths containing spaces, `$`, backticks, `;`, etc. make the returned “exact next call” incorrect or injectable; the operands must be quoted or the command should be built as an argv list.

chunk_findings.detail: The module bootstraps imports by inserting only the repository root (`parents[1]`) into `sys.path`, then imports sibling test helpers as top-level modules (`conftest`, `submodule_fixture`). If the `tests` directory is not already on `sys.path` — for example under `pytest --import-mode=importlib`, or if `tests/` is a package so pytest inserts the repository root rather than the test directory — collection fails at the `from conftest import ...` / `from submodule_fixture import ...` lines with `ModuleNotFoundError` for `conftest` or `submodule_fixture`. The inserted path should include `parents[0]` (the `tests` directory) or the helpers should be imported as a package, otherwise the test file cannot be collected in those environments.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_literal(sub)` is only applied to the overlap pattern; `_is_inside(glob, sub)` still compares against the raw submodule path, so submodule paths containing glob metacharacters are not read literally for the “is this glob inside the submodule?” test. With a submodule path literally `vendor/*`, the escaped glob `vendor/[*]/**` is wholly inside that submodule, but `_is_inside` returns False because the string does not start with the raw prefix `vendor/*/`, and `GL.overlap` then returns True against `_literal('vendor/*') + '/**'` (`vendor/[*]/**`). `_spans` therefore reports a crossing and the guard refuses a valid claim. Conversely, the unescaped glob `vendor/*/**` is treated as inside because it starts with the raw `vendor/*/`, even though its `*` also matches other immediate children such as `vendor/other/file`, so a crossing lease is not refused.

chunk_findings.detail: `_pair_calls` constructs the suggested inner-item glob as `sub + "/**"` and then only applies `shlex.quote`. chunk_findings.detail: The new `stray` remediation chooses `"<submodule path>.stray"` as the move-aside target without checking for collision. If the repository has both a stray submodule `vendor` and a real submodule `vendor.stray`, the generated command is `mv vendor vendor.stray && ...`. POSIX `mv` treats an existing directory target as a directory to move *into*, so this succeeds and leaves the stray files under `vendor.stray/vendor`, i.e. inside another submodule’s worktree, before running `git submodule update --init --recursive`. That can silently pollute or mis-scope `vendor.stray`; if `vendor.stray` is a file, the command instead fails.

chunk_findings.detail: The stray remediation’s collision avoidance is filesystem-only. The intended “caller asks for a free name” behavior is not encoded in the returned command, so any caller that treats `Problem.fix` as an executable remediation command gets wrong behavior.
